speechtext:

Okotie-Eboh, the Nigerian minister of finance, Hon. Z. B. Dipcharima, minister of commerce and industry, Hon. J. C. Obande, acting minister of works, and ministers from the three regions of Nigeria who represent their country on this mission.

Northern Affairs and National Resources. My question is prompted by a lady corespondent-
Oh, oh.

-correspondent. In view of the historic interest of the site where Dollard des Ormeaux defended Montreal, located at the foot of the Long Sault rapids just east of Hawkesbury on what is known as the old Ross farm, and in view of the fact this site will soon be lost by flooding due to the Quebec hydro project under way at Carillon, would the minister indicate what representations have been made to the Quebec government or Quebec hydro to have this site protected from inundation?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. G. Dinsdale (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I am grateful to the hon. member for having given me notice of this question, which involves considerable research. I wish I were as sure as he that the Ross farm site is in fact the site where Dollard des Ormeaux is said to have fought so heroically the battle of the Long Sault. This is one of the most stirring pages in Canadian history, and if it were possible to bring this page to life once again through a positive identification of the actual site, I assure the hon. member that I would want to explore all possible ways to preserve it as a part of our national historic heritage.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that at best the Ross farm site can only be said to be one of a number of possible locations where the battle may have taken place. A large body of archaeological opinion favours the Carillon site as the actual location. Historians support the viewpoint that Dollard's last stand took place at the western end of the lac des Deux Montagnes.
Mr. Thomas Lee has done some thorough archaeological investigation of the Ross farm site. The evidence unearthed is extremely interesting from a general archaeological standpoint. However, the artifacts located there do not go back beyond the early nineteenth century and indicate that the site in all likelihood was a portage encampment, one of the several portages on this reach of the Ottawa river.
This background information has been made available to both the Ontario and Quebec governments. However, in view of the inconclusive evidence I feel I have no justifiable grounds to attempt to delay the progress of the Carillon dam construction project through representations to the government of Quebec or the Quebec hydro electric commission.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, July 12, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-71, respecting the civil service of Canada -Mr. Fleming (Eglinton)-Mr. McCleave in the chair.

On clause 1-Short title.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee adjourned yesterday I was speaking on clause 1. In reading Hansard this morning I note that part of my remarks, where I was referring to the 1918 act, are reported without any interruptions. I regret that the enrichment offered by way of interruption of those remarks by the hon. member for Greenwood is not recorded for posterity. My remarks had relation to certain interjections he was making, and it is regrettable that the interjections are not on record. However, perhaps he will put the substance of them on record later in this debate.
In the concluding part of my remarks I was dealing with the matter of bilingualism as it had been treated by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm and the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot. I had suggested to them that I thought their treatment of the subject was not as objective as the subject itself, a very important one, deserves, or as objective as the members of the special committee were in dealing with the matter.
The point I was seeking to make, with particular reference to the remarks of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, was that he had confused references to the two languages or to bilingualism with racial or ethnic origin, which is not the point at issue. The special committee attempted to deal with the subject of the necessity in this country of in fact using two languages as required, and it accepted the proposition that the spirit of confederation on this point had to be honoured. That was the approach of the committee, and I thought it was a very good one.
In dealing with the matter the hon. member did not treat it in that way at all. He spoke about the ethnic origin of certain persons in the civil service. So far as I know the civil service commission has never been charged with the responsibility of ascertaining the ethnic origin of Canadians being employed by them, and I for one hope that will never be the basis of selection for the civil service of Canada but that the basis of selection will be merit and the test of citizenship or ethnic origin merely Canadianism.
In other words the only proposition I can accept on that subject is that once a person becomes a Canadian citizen he is a Canadian citizen with full rights, and there are no distinctions as among Canadian citizens. Perhaps it is a trite way of putting it, but I take the position that once we have citizenship no matter by what process, whether through naturalization or by birth, we are Canadians one and all and we must not be kept in separate categories by reason of

ethnic origin. For that reason I was seeking to make a critical reference to the hon. member's argument on the question of bilingualism.
If I understood his French correctly, and on this point I think I did, it seemed to me that he was referring to French Canadians much of the time instead of referring to the French language and the necessity for bilingualism. To me there is a very important distinction. If he merely used the terms interchangeably or carelessly I have no objection, but if he was seeking to use the terms deliberately to indicate that the civil service commission must seek to ascertain the ethnic origin of persons being selected for positions I would take objection to that and say that the test must remain bilingualism, that that test alone is the proper one and ethnic origin is not the test.
The subject is a large one and quite complex. The committee did have some rather good presentations made to it. Le conseil de la vie francaise made a presentation and I thought the discussion in the committee on the whole subject was very good. I also want to point out one other weakness in their case. They took certain segments of the civil service and tried to make a statistical approach to the numbers who are bilingual in given branches. The weakness of that should be readily apparent. If you take a small branch you can come up with statistics that will show that practically all speak one or the other of the two languages.
It must be acknowledged that the necessity for the two languages is greater in some parts of the country than in others. There are problems like that. The point I wish to make is that if the statistical approach is to be used, the over-all picture must be considered. They should not select one branch or another. When that is done problems arise. You may be dealing with technical subjects in relation to which the educational system throughout the country is such that applicants from one part of Canada would seem to enjoy preference because their educational qualifications better suit them for certain positions.
This problem is interrelated with the whole question of education and training. I hope we can develop a solution to the problem on a broad scale. I hope the development of the solution will take full cognizance of the need for encouraging educational institutions in various parts of the country to provide the type of education that will better qualify applicants for some positions. I believe all hon. members would agree there is need for more and better training in the field of public administration as well as in the technical and scientific fields, and that this has a bearing
Civil Service Act
on the number of bilingual persons employed through the civil service in any particular branch. That is all I shall say on that subject for the moment.
Mr. Chairman, before the hon. member passes to another subject, would he indicate at what page I may find the reference to the remarks he attributed to me a while ago.
I listened to the hon. member's speech very carefully. I have not marked my Hansard because I did not receive it in time to peruse it.

I rise only to point out that the hon. member appears to be confusing me with the hon. member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm. I think the hon. gentleman has attributed to me words used by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm, words which I have not uttered in this chamber.

I am quite satisfied to accept the hon. member's explanation in toto. If I have in any way attributed to him words he did not utter I completely withdraw my reference. The hon. member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm, when speaking, did raise the question in my mind. It may have been merely a careless reference on his part or it may have been intentional. The point is that if it was an intentional reference I wished to direct attention to the approach I feel should be taken in this matter. I wished to reveal my views on the point. I believe it is an important point in the long term, because it is related to a continuing situation and is dependent upon many factors, one of which is education.
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strath-cona delivered a speech in which he seemed to indicate that he desired more direct ministerial control of the civil service. I was unable to gather how far he wanted to go in this respect. I regret that the hon. gentleman is not here to hear my remarks on this point. His comments were certainly capable of giving rise to the interpretation I mention. He appeared to be pressing for more direct patronage influence in appointments. If he did not mean that, I have no desire to insist on placing that interpretation on his remarks. On the other hand, if he did mean it I wish to point out to him that the original Civil Service Act attempted to get away from that sort of thing. I think it is the desire of most hon. members in all quarters of the house to continue to avoid controls of that nature. If I am correct in interpreting the hon. gentleman's remarks as representing a plea to return to that condition, I would

Civil Service Act
expect that hon. members on both sides of the house would not desire to support the hon. member's position.
There are many references in the bill to matters of major importance with which one is tempted to deal. One of the most important is that of the relationship between the government and staff organizations in the civil service. This represents a difficult and complex problem with which we shall deal in a detailed way when we consider clause 7.
Clause 7 as sent to the special committee was in my view inadequate. The committee was successful in having an amendment inserted, and the bill as it now appears before us is considerably improved over the bill that was sent to the committee in so far as the question of staff consultations is concerned. A long argument could be developed concerning whether or not the procedure for staff consultations is adequate. I do not like the word consult in that context, because I think it is imprecise and inadequate. I shall argue that point a little later.
Clause 10 relates to the subject of pay and allowances. This clause together with clause 7 raises the old question of the rights of civil service bodies to negotiate, to engage in arbitration and other related rights which may be discussed on the specific clauses. Another matter that is raised is this. Once this bill becomes law I feel it should be reviewed from time to time by a committee of this house. When I say "from time to time" I mean reasonably frequently because we are, through the growth of the civil service, moving into a period when the concepts of the civil service and of arbitration are changing. I am not wholly satisfied with the clauses as they now exist in the bill, and wish to see how they operate. I am grateful to the extent that they modernize the act, but I wish to see them examined and kept under constant review. If the government continues to have responsibility in this field, which I expect it will not in the light of forthcoming events, I hope the question of pay and allowances will be kept under constant review. Government needs to be ever watchful of the independence of the civil service commission.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, before the hon. member departs from that point would he be good enough to indicate how frequently he thinks review should be made? The hon. gentleman has raised an interesting point. I am sure it would be useful if on the basis of the hon. gentleman's experience he would indicate to the committee how frequently review should be made. Would the hon. gentleman suggest that it should take place every five or ten years?

I do not think it would be proper to give a dogmatic answer to that question in terms of a precise number of years. In a period when the cost of living is increasing and salaries reflect those increases, the question of pay and allowances becomes of acute interest and requires review more frequently than in a period when the cost of living is static and pay and allowances do not constitute an acute problem. If government is careful in its relationships with the civil service the need of review is not as urgent as it is when government is careless in those relationships. In any event, I am not talking about an annual review. I also think ten years would be much too long a time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are talking about a review of the act.
If the hon. member wants to crowd me into a somewhat dogmatic answer, I would say that probably three to five years might be the period of time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We are not talking about review of pay and allowances.
No; review of the act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We are talking about review of the act and procedures in the act.
It was a review of the act I was talking about. I picked out the pay and allowances matter only as an illustration of the type of subject that could be important.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Quite so.

I want to make that clear; it is review of this whole act. The clause of the Heeney report I wanted to read is this. By the way, I should at this point make it clear that the Heeney commission was a commission or process started by the former government and continued by this government. In debate yesterday there seemed to be some confusion on that point, but I think there is nothing at issue on it.
Paragraph 61 on page 23 of that report of the civil service commission of Canada on personnel administration in the public service reads as follows:
Although it is not, perhaps, widely appreciated, it seems to us that the independent status of the commission in matters of pay and conditions of work is as important a characteristic of our system as its independence in relation to appointment and promotion. In its recommendations on pay, the commission is no more subject to government direction than it is to influence by organized employees. It is as immune to outside pressures as the law can make it. Its sole duty is to reach, within the framework of accepted principles, conclusions based on objective examination and analysis through its pay research bureau and such other sources as may be available to it.

What I wanted to point out here was the need for constant vigilance in order to see that this condition continues. This is a very important matter. I do not wish to rethresh old straw, but I had a difference of opinion with the Minister of Finance having to do with this very subject. Regrettably we did not have an opportunity of debating that matter fully because of the form in which the matter came before the house. However,
I thought he was less objective or less vigilant than I would have wished him to be in his appreciation of the necessity for preserving the independence of the civil service commission on this point and related points.
Holding that view, I wish to stress again the necessity for continuing and continuous vigilance to preserve the independence of the civil service commission in its work. If we do not do that; if it becomes a mere agency of government as opposed to an independent commission with its independent guarantee in its performance of the duties with respect to the public service which it is created to perform, then we will have indeed indirectly undone the very thing we are seeking to do and to continue by this legislation.
There is another point of considerable importance that I wish to mention. Of necessity the authority of deputy ministers has been increased. My colleague the hon. member for Ottawa East yesterday put on record the dangers arising from patronage within the service. While we have in this bill increased the powers of deputy ministers and deputy heads of departments, I am not convinced that we have come up with a wholly satisfactory solution by way of appeal procedures to protect all civil servants against improper use of that power. In setting up appeal procedures and methods of protecting individual civil servants against the abuse of that power it is very easy to get a cumbersome kind of system that will impede the work being done and the internal efficiency of administering the service. There is presented a complex problem which I recognize at once.
On that point I am not satisfied that the bill as presented embodies a wholly happy conclusion. I shall therefore content myself now with asking for continued vigilance on the part of all members of the House of Commons to see that, if administration of the act reveals the necessity for a strengthening of the appeal, arbitration and related procedures in relation to this subject, the bill is brought back to this house or forced back to this house and the necessary action taken. From my point of view I thought our solutions were not quite as adequate as they should have been, and there is considerable doubt and uncertainty in my own mind as to just what the future holds in that respect.
Civil Service Act
I hope my fears in this connection will never be realized' but will be proved wrong. None the less, I would be less than frank if I did not say that they were there. I observe that my time has expired, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Go ahead.
There are some other remarks that perhaps could be made.

The
hon. member's time has now expired. Is it the pleasure of the committee to give further time to the hon. member?
Agreed.

I do not wish to abuse the good nature of the committee on this question of using more time than is provided by the rules. However, I have a few more remarks to make and I will try to abbreviate them.
There is the question of holidays. Changes had to be made for two main reasons. There are new problems in this field. The new problems arise out of the universal acceptance of the five day week since the original act was passed. It seems to me that a great many members of the committee failed to realize that the five day week, as a universally accepted proposition, is really in the final analysis comparatively new in relation to the 42-year history of the former act. It is something that has developed only since the end of the war and really in the last very few years. That consideration presents new problems in drafting legislation on the subject of holidays.
Then there is another problem that has arisen in connection with holidays. I refer to the very swift expansion of the civil service, particularly during the second great war. The civil service has gone into activities which, by their very nature, involve shift work and work of that nature other than office work to a far greater extent than was the case at the time of the 1918 act. Those two changes, with the effluxion of time, have created problems in relation to holidays for the different segments of the public service of Canada. When you are dealing with administrative staff and office staff it is quite a simple problem, but it can become a very complex problem where you are dealing with shift work, overtime pay and other related facets of the subject.
I am not sure that our committee came up with an adequate solution of that problem. I hope that again the commission under the regulations will be able to work out something that is satisfactory. We had some reference to this problem in the House of Commons in connection with the Post Office Department. I put a question to the Postmaster

Civil Service Act
General in relation to the July 1 holiday, which happened to fall on a Saturday this year. I thought his answer was less than adequate or satisfactory in dealing with that matter. It points up the need for a thorough job of work to be done by the commisison in working out the kind of regulations that will grant the holidays that are in accordance with our modern ideas on this matter of employees having to work overtime hours on holidays and allow them the necessary overtime pay or compensatory leave. It is a complex problem and there is perhaps no point in pursuing it further at this moment, other than to indicate that in my view the committee did not by any means reach a wholly complete or satisfactory answer on the subject. I hope the commission may succeed, through regulations and application of the legislation, in doing what the legislation itself may have failed to do.
There is one other major problem with which I think I should deal. It arises under one clause of the bill only but it does have general application to the whole civil service. I refer to the provision in the legislation having to do with the appointment to the civil service of ministers' secretaries and executive assistants. The bill contains a clause that as far as I am concerned is quite unsatisfactory. I want to deal with it here only in its relationship to the general problems of civil service administration. I will have further remarks to make on the subject when we come to the particular clause.
Under the bill as now resubmitted to the house, ministers' secretaries and executive assistants are eligible for appointment to the civil service after three years' service. The former legislation provided only for secretaries. I have no objection to enlarging that provision to provide for both private secretaries and executive assistants, but I must issue a warning on this one point. I think experience and an objective examination of this subject will back me up.
It now becomes possible for a government through this back door method, if I may use the term, to place some 40 new civil servants in the public service of Canada each year after the government has been in office three years. I think there has not been a sufficient realization of the significance of this provision. It does not take many appointments of this kind to lower the morale in a particular department, because they interfere with the expectancy of promotion. If this power were to be used as is provided in the bill before us, it could indeed do much to destroy morale in the civil service. The point-
May I ask the hon. member a question?

Perhaps the hon. member would just bear with me for a moment. The existing legislation has one limitation in this regard. This is not a precise way of expressing the limitation, but it is that when a minister leaves the department or dies-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no limitation now on the number of people.
There is no limitation on the number of people, but in the existing legislation it is limited to one secretary-and if I may use this term, that cuts it in half-when a minister leaves a department.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No.

I will be coming to the precise terms of the act in a moment. I have the act here. My point refers to this removal of any limitation on the right to appoint those persons. I think it is important that those persons have the right to be appointed. However, I think that right should be subject to a further limitation, something in the nature of the death of a minister, a minister leaving a portfolio or leaving the government, something of that sort, so it would not be possible to have a continuing flow of ministers' secretaries and executive assistants from a particular minister in charge of a particular portfolio into this channel.
I am open to suggestion on the form of that limitation, but I think there should be a limitation in the clause of the bill similar to the former one; otherwise it could be very harmful to the morale of the civil service and much damage could be done to the civil service by this clause as it now stands.
The hon. member for Greenwood had a question he wished to ask me on the point, and I am afraid I cut him off.

My question was just this. Is the figure of 40 used by the hon. member a theoretical figure, or is it an actual, realistic figure? Does that not imply that people holding these positions are going to be resigning year by year by year? It is just the figure of 40 that I wish to understand.
It is only a round figure. There are 22 cabinet ministers and the Leader of the Opposition, making 23 in all. The number could be 46 right now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: After three years.
Yes, but the government has been in office three years now. There could be 46 of these persons at the moment, and immediately this bill is passed-
No.

Would the hon. member hear me out, please. If I am correct in the

number of cabinet ministers, 46 of these appointments could be made the day after this bill becomes law. Then you could repeat that process-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is after three years.

I wish to differ with the hon. member for Carleton. I was trying to avoid dealing with this difference at this stage;
I would rather do it on the clause. The difference turns on interpretation. The difference between the hon. member for Carleton and myself is this. The hon. member for Carleton says this could only happen each three years. I differ in my opinion on that. I say it could happen more frequently; I say it could happen every year. In any event, even if the hon. member is right my point is still the same if this could happen every three years.
For the purpose of answering the question asked by the hon. member for Greenwood I wonder whether I could take an illustration. I see the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is in her seat, and I am sure the charming lady would not mind if I used her for the purpose of illustrating this point. Immediately this bill became law she could have two persons put into her department under this provision. I presume they would be appointed to her department. That is a reasonable assumption based on past experience. She could have two persons appointed. That is a proper thing from the point of view of those persons and I do not quarrel with that. However, we must realize that it does interfere with the expectancy of promotion within the department.
Of course if the minister were moving to another portfolio, if she were moving to the other place or leaving the government for one reason or another, these private secretaries and executive assistants would be left in a very awkward position after devoted service in the public service of Canada. I wish to make it very clear that I have no objection to them being appointed in those circumstances, but if this method were used by the minister-and I do not suggest she would have any such motive-as a means of putting persons into her department, it could be quite badly abused and could destroy the morale of the department or be very harmful to it.
I do not know how many executive assistants the minister has, but she could have more than one. I wish to point out that the legislation does not restrict her; there is no statutory restriction on the number of private secretaries she may have, as I read the whole of the legislation. That comes to the nub of the difference in point of view between the hon. member for Carleton and myself. If the
Civil Service Act
minister has more than one private secretary, she could keep this process going indefinitely. If she has only one, of course she would have to appoint another person, and she could only repeat the process every three years. But even that would be a very severe thing. Suppose she were minister for six years. She might have put four persons into the department, and that could be a very severe blow to the morale of the department. As a matter of fact the hon. lady might take the case of the previous government, which was in office for about 22 years. Even accepting the argument used by the hon. member for Carleton it can be seen that some ministers could have appointed 14 persons to the department. In my view there is no doubt that this would have totally destroyed morale in the department, because it would have removed the expectancy of promotion on the part of departmental employees.
So this is a point which is of major importance to the whole subject, an importance which it is perhaps not appreciated by some hon. members. I do not hesitate to say it should be dealt with when we come to the clause concerned and that some restriction should be placed on this right to appoint. It should at least be made dependent on the minister leaving his portfolio, or leaving the ministry.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Does the hon. member not agree with me that the phrase "for which he is qualified" would have an effect on this procedure?

No. It has a very limited effect. It is not a significant protection. That means he is coming in from outside the department. Let us assume, for the sake of argument, that we have a person within the department besides the minister's appointee, and that they are both equally qualified. The effect of placing the minister's secretary in the department removes the expectancy of promotion from the one already in the department who may have had every right to expect a promotion.
So this right to appoint ministers' secretaries is something which must be carefully used or it could be very harmful. The bill as it is submitted to us and as it is now before the committee, has removed some of the restrictions which were formerly part of the law on this point. I am not recommending that we should return to the precise wording of the former legislation, because the former legislation is too narrow in that the right was restricted to the appointment of one person.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. The hon. gentleman has said on a number of occasions that the former legislation restricted such appointments to one. But he is, of course, aware of

Civil Service Act
the ruling of the Department of Justice which indicated that the expression "private secretary" included associate private secretaries and assistant private secretaries. The net result was that there was no restriction in the old legislation on the number of persons from a minister's office who could enter the civil service through that channel.

Yes. I think the hon. member for Carleton will agree with me that what is attempted in the bill is to be more precise with regard to the point he has mentioned. The measure is, in that respect, an improvement because the language used is more precise and direct. I may say that in 1918, as far as I can find, the term "executive assistant" was rarely heard of. It is like so many titles placed on jobs in the service, some of which are new and ingenious. In any event it is a very popular title now.
I have no objection at all to the bill covering the two persons in the minister's office. I think these persons in the minister's office should be completely and adequately protected. But I think, consistent with doing that, it is not necessary to put in any language which is so loose as to be capable of permitting an abuse. One minister abusing this clause and taking advantage of the opportunity to use it improperly could practically destroy morale in the whole department, and that would be a most serious thing to do. It would materially hamper the effectiveness or the efficiency of any government.
I wish to thank the committee for granting me the indulgence of extra time, and in closing I should like to repeat the reference I made at the beginning of my remarks to the objectivity of those hon. members who served on the special committee which dealt with this subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on the subject. I really do not think the hon. member has any reason for concern in the situation he has envisaged. I can assure him, and I believe my colleagues are in much the same position as I am, that competent executive assistants and private secretaries are so hard to come by that we are not anxious to have them leave our offices for employment in the department. Moreover, any employment within the department which would be attractive to them would be on a level where there would certainly be major competition.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I should just like to make a correction in yesterday's Hansard, when I spoke on this bill. My correction applies to both the French and English versions of the official report.

As reported on page 5 of the appendix to Hansard for July 12, 1961, the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) asked me to repeat the exact figure which I quoted to the house a few moments earlier as to the average French-Canadian representation.
At the time, I thought he was asking me in what proportion the French-Canadian representation had fallen off during the period from 1950-1958. In the case of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, the figure was 0.7 per cent. That is the figure I quoted to indicate the French-Canadian representation in that department. That is not correct, since I know that as far as that department is concerned, the proportion of bilingual Canadians has increased, though I do not remember by how much.
(Text):

I should like to make one or two general observations with respect to statements which have been made by hon. members, with a view to eliminating as far as possible any sense of discrimination because of language, race, colour, creed or religion.
We are, of course, proud that Canadian civil servants enjoy such a world-wide and eminent reputation for honesty and integrity. We are all proud of that whenever we travel and have occasion to talk to people abroad. We are happy, and justly proud, to learn of the fine reputations that our civil servants enjoy. I am sure, too, that the civil servants themselves wish to be completely sure that at no time does the question of discrimination creep into any of the considerations which come before them.
I see from Votes and Proceedings of June 26 that the standing committee has recommended an amendment which deals to some extent with the subject. I am not speaking directly to that particular clause, but I would point out in a general way that the amendment addresses itself to the civil service commission. It calls upon the civil service commission not to discriminate against any person by reason of race, national origin, colour or religion. This applies to the commission itself.
To my way of thinking that amendment is perhaps a little superfluous. It is, perhaps, not necessary; but I am satisfied to have such an amendment on the record, though I have seen nothing to indicate why it should be called for. I suggest generally that a precautionary measure of the same sort should be taken with respect to the civil servants themselves. There was an incident a short while ago when a civil servant expressed himself in a way which could indicate that he might practise discrimination. I hope, as

we come to consider this bill clause by clause, that I may have the opportunity to introduce an amendment to remedy that situation.
Members of the civil service very often occupy positions in which they have to make judgments and decisions in respect to matters which come before them. If a civil servant has any prejudices because of colour, race or religion, this would impinge upon his sense of impartiality. Therefore we should, if we possibly can, address ourselves to the civil service to prevent individuals from exercising or practising any form of discrimination. That is the observation I wanted to make in addressing myself to the civil service, against whom I say there is no criticism to be levelled in this regard. It was just the one incident which happened which led me to mention this subject, because it could provoke among members of parliament the fear that if there is one such individual there could well be others.
As I indicated a moment ago, and I propose to offer an amendment, the act should perhaps contain a provision that if any civil servant practises discrimination or is known to practise discrimination because of race, colour, creed or religion he shall be deemed to have exposed himself to the dangers of sanction and, perhaps, dismissal as a civil servant. I hope the committee will bear with me in this regard, because it is not a matter of politics or any consideration other than that which should be unanimous among members of parliament.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few words I should like to express at this time with respect to this particular measure. I want to associate myself first with others who have been calling on the government to accord to civil servants the right of bargaining collectively with the appropriate arms of the government in order to establish hours of work, salaries, holidays and other associated working conditions.
I should like to pay tribute to Canada's public service. I believe there has been developed in this country over the years a civil service which is second to none. I think we have within that service many thousands of citizens who are devoting their talents with, on some occasions, real sacrifice to the public good. I think all members of parliament from time to time should acknowledge the very great service that is being rendered our nation by these our public employees.
I do regret very much that at times there seems to be widespread condemnation of the public service, and regret that hon. members sometimes use words that might be interpreted as a general assault upon the civil service. I should like to take exception to
Civil Service Act
the words of the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona, because I feel he made rather sweeping charges about our civil service. At one point in his statement he was talking about the former government becoming arrogant, and then went on to say as reported at page 7966 of Hansard for July 12, 1961:
The whole service had got a little too stuck in that way of doing business. In some respects it had taken on some of the characteristics of its bosses, and a complete change was needed.
I do not think there is any ground whatsoever for such a general accusation. I have had a very moderate amount of business with the civil service, yet have not noticed any change in the attitude of public servants with the change in administration. I think a public servant who is a good public servant before a change in government is an equally good public servant after a change in the administration. Rather than tearing down public servants I think we should acknowledge what is the fact, namely that Canada has built a civil service that is a credit to this nation, a civil service that should be defended by members of parliament.
I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary whether he can inform the committee as to what encouragement in general is being given by the government to bilingualism in the civil service. Statistics have been placed on the record from time to time, and it will not be necessary to repeat them in detail, as to the proportion of civil servants who are bilingual in the various departments. Some of these statistics are contained in the "memoire du conseil de la vie frangaise", which was presented to the standing committee of this house, at pages 7 and 8 of that presentation.
I do not speak this morning to hurl any widespread criticism at this government or any former government, but merely rise to express the point of view that in a nation which is bilingual, with approximately one third of its citizens of French origin, we should be able to give greater recognition to this basic fact than we have been able to do as a nation to date, particularly in respect to the statistics regarding our civil service.
The statistics to which I refer comprise a comparison between 1951 and 1958, showing the changes which have taken place. Whether those changes tend to meet the point I make to some extent, or move further away, they cannot be blamed wholly on this administration, nor am I endeavouring to blame them wholly on the former administration. I should like to know, however, whether the parliamentary secretary can indicate any up to date statistics in respect to the proportion of civil servants of the various departments who are bilingual. I should like to know whether there

Civil Service Act
are statistics available beyond 1958 which establish a trend since that year toward bilingualism among our civil servants.
When the committee met the hon. member tor Timiskaming made what I thought was a very constructive suggestion. He suggested that real encouragement should be given to civil servants in all departments, working and resident in all parts ol Canada, to become bilingual, and that they should be allowed as part of their working time to take a certain number of hours per week in order to become fluent in the language other than their mother tongue. This kind of program would not only increase bilingualism in Canada but would give Canada's civil servants who are not bilingual an opportunity to acquire this facility in order to better serve our nation.
I should like the parliamentary secretary to inform this committee whether there are any particular plans in existence which the government is now implementing to increase bilingualism in our civil service. I think members of parliament in all parties agree that Canada is a bilingual nation, and I for one feel that French Canadians have a justifiable complaint that their language, particularly in this respect, has not been given the proper consideration by this or by former administrations. I think they are justified in feeling that, whether deliberately or otherwise, there has been discrimination against them.
I think we must recognize that there is a problem, and that all of us should do our best to see that it is dealt with and that there is the kind of equal recognition which I think members of parliament in all parties support. Therefore when I resume my seat I hope the parliamentary secretary can inform the committee now, when we are considering this bill, what plans the government has in hand to increase bilingualism in the civil service.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to revert to the subject that was under discussion between the hon. member for Ottawa West and the parliamentary secretary when I came into the chamber a little while ago. I do so without apology of any kind because, like the parliamentary secretary and perhaps unlike anyone else in the house, I have had some experience of being in the kind of position to which the hon. member for Ottawa West referred.
It is true that when I ceased to be head of the prime minister's office I did not avail myself of any rights I might have had under the Civil Service Act. Neither did the hon. member for Carleton. We both chose to follow a different path or were chosen to follow a different path; I am not sure which way I should put it. While I was head of the prime

minister's office for the period from 1945 to 1952, I had the feeling then and even after I went into public life, about which hon. gentlemen opposite may be incredulous, that the Liberal party like all things here below was not going to be eternally in office and that some day some problems would arise in respect of the staffs of ministers' offices. I recognized the feeling of the straight line civil servants-and I think the hon. member for Ottawa West put their concern very clearly- when someone from this "tainted" world in which the hon. member for Carleton and I lived for so long is put into a department and apparently blocks the promotion of a hard working, conscientious public servant.
I also think we should recognize what the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration pointed out a little while ago, that our government cannot function at all under our system unless ministers, who in these days when the state intervenes to such a degree in every aspect of life have terrible problems and responsibilities, are adequately assisted by competent staffs in their offices because otherwise they cannot do their work well. It is not fair to the people who are to staff these offices-and in fact in this competitive world it will not happen except for a few rare and conscientious people like the hon. member for Carleton and myself-to expect them to stay there very long when they can get more stable and secure positions elsewhere.
I do not count the fact that I stayed so long as evidence of any virtue on my part, because I had a good time when I was in the public service and I enjoyed it, although perhaps I did not have quite as good a time as I have had since then, but a computation was made once, and if I had just remained in the Department of External Affairs-where I was appointed under the merit system, I might say, in 1937-assuming that I would have received normal promotions from 1937 to 1952 and no favouritism my income would have been considerably higher than in fact it was. A friend of mine found that out for me, because I really was not that much interested. I had made the hypothesis one day and he made a computation covering two or three people who had entered the service at the same time I had, and they were all better off. I am not citing this as any virtue, because I think I had a better time than they had. They had to live abroad in other countries while I was able to go on living in Ottawa and doing the things that I enjoyed doing very much.
The real reason I am bringing up this matter is that I think it is essential to the proper functioning of our system of government that ministers have competent staffs,

and they will not get them unless there is some provision for a reasonable measure of security for those staffs in the case of a change of government or a change of minister. I think the hon. member for Ottawa West is quite right that security should not be provided in the act for someone who remains in such service for only a couple of years and then leaves because the minister does not get on very well with him. The minister is going to stay on, and it is quite wrong that such a person should be put in a slot in the civil service. If the minister has made a mistake and the person is not suitable, the unsuitable person should not be put in the civil service. That is quite wrong.
But it does seem to me that there should be maximum security consistent with efficiency in the service, which must always be the first consideration, when there is a change of government or a change of minister; because it would be quite unreasonable to expect a new minister to accept all the staff of an out-going minister. It often happens that they do, but they should not be expected to have to do so. One minister does things in one way and another in another way, and they should be able to make such arrangements that they can do their own jobs in the most efficient manner possible.
I also venture to discuss this matter for another reason. I have believed for a long time, long before I came to this side of the house and, indeed, long before I ever entered public life and while I was still a public servant, that it is not merely ministers who need adequate, competent and efficient staffs. I do not think that political parties in opposition which have an essential duty to perform, a duty that has never been more necessary than in recent times, should have to be dependent upon political funds to provide the staff to enable them to do the work they are expected to do in this house. I cannot think of a better expenditure of public moneys.
I may say that I preached this doctrine when I was a minister, and I preached it before I was a minister. I was not able to convince my colleagues, though anyone who will trace the history of the office of leader of the opposition from the time Mr. St. Laurent became prime minister will see that repeated and steady ameliorations were made in that regard. I do not think they were good enough and Mr. St. Laurent knew at the time that I did not think so. Indeed, I am sure he would not in the least mind my saying that on one or two occasions I urged that much more should be done. It is just as important that the staff of the leader of an opposition should be protected and given security as the staffs
Civil Service Act
of ministers. I understand that in the legislation they are, and that is as it should be. I know something about this, too, because I have had some practical experience of this matter. I think the committee might be interested in this. It shows how important it is for us, in carrying out our arrangements in parliament, to have a civilized way of dealing with these problems.
It so happened that some time after the late Gordon Graydon had ceased to be the leader of the opposition he went on one occasion to Mr. St. Laurent and pointed out that he had failed to take certain technical steps which should have been taken to protect the position, under the Civil Service Act, of the successor of my hon. friend from Carleton. At that time I was the head of Mr. St. Laurent's office. Mr. St. Laurent asked me if steps could not be taken, notwithstanding the fact that the law had not in fact been carried out, to make sure that the position was protected.
I am very glad to say that the civil service commission took a very liberal view, if I may use that word, and I insist that it be with a small "1", Mr. Chairman. The commission made a very liberal interpretation of the law and the position was adequately protected. That gentleman, I might add parenthetically, was quite properly devoting a good part of his activities at that time to an effort to overthrow the government then in office, as he should have been doing. Steps were taken to see that his position was adequately protected.
Then came a day some years later when that same gentleman no longer seemed to meet the requirements of his political chief, the then leader of the opposition. I am mentioning no names in relating this incident, but this is what happened. Because the leader of the opposition had not changed and because it was the same man for whom he had been working for some time, technically again he had no rights under the Civil Service Act. However, the matter was brought to the attention of the government of that day. It was brought to the attention of my hon. friend Mr. Harris, and by him to the attention of the prime minister. Again a liberal view was taken. Notwithstanding the technicalities of the act, provision was made in the civil service for that distinguished Canadian who had been for a long time the secretary to the leader of the opposition. Provision was made by the civil service commission with the concurrence and active encouragement of the then minister of citizenship and immigration, Mr. Harris, who provided him with a position in his own

Civil Service Act
department considerably above what the technical requirements of the law would have called for.
Very shortly after this event occurred I succeeded Mr. Harris in that department. I may say that notwithstanding his political affiliation, which had never been concealed and which was never concealed from that time on, he served in that department with the utmost distinction and loyalty. His service could not have been finer. In addition to that he served with the high degree of competence that I am sure he displayed with whoever he served. I had many loyal civil servants- and indeed I never knew of any who were not-in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration when I was the minister. I consider there was none more loyal and few who showed more initiative than the gentleman to whom I am referring.
This is the civilized way to do things. When the government changed, of course, the new administration felt it could use the services of that gentleman in a somewhat more "tainted" way-to use the word I previously used, again with quotation marks-as the hon. member for Carleton and I had served at one time, and he is serving in that way now, no doubt doing his utmost to further the fortunes of the government he is serving, as he should be doing.
I relate this experience because I think it illustrates the civilized way of handling these matters. I do not claim any credit for myself in all this because I was a public servant, I think, when these transactions occurred. Nevertheless the incident I have related illustrates the broad spirit in which Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Harris viewed these matters. When I hear some of the things that are said about public servants in this house now, I cannot refrain from drawing that contrast.
In that context let me say this, in which I think the hon. member for Assiniboia will be very interested. I do not think what I propose to do is against the rules, because what I should like to read does not relate to the debate we are now having but to something else, though it is extremely pertinent to my remarks. I have in my hand today's Globe and Mail which carries an editorial entitled "The Government and the Establishment" from which I propose to read part of a paragraph. I could read a sentence uncomplimentary to the present government, but I am not going to do that. I shall read just a portion of the editorial which sets out a so-called question of principle or practice. Referring to the present government, the editorial states:
When it came to power in 1957, it succeeded a Liberal regime which had held office continuously for more than two decades. During that long period

the higher, policy making posts of the civil service and the crown agencies, had been filled by men who, while not necessarily political partisans-
I might pause just to recall that two of them were Mr. Justice McTague and Mr. Henry Borden. I continue:
-were in sympathy with the policies of the King and St. Laurent regimes, and shared their conviction that Canada's economic health depended on the continuance of heavy taxation and tight restrictions on credit and business.
I congratulate the writer for having discerned something that has been very difficult for the Canadian people to discern and with which he deals in the following sentence:
The Conservatives, by contrast, favoured tax reduction, easier credit, and other policies designed to promote economic expansion.
I must say that anything more ironic, more Alice in Wonderlandish, in relation to what has really happened in the last few weeks, would be exceedingly difficult to imagine. The following is the sentence I particularly wish to draw to the attention of the committee:
But they found themselves compelled to work through a bureaucracy which was highly sceptical of these ideas and which yearned to maintain its accustomed ways.
I remember very well the days of transition in 1957. After all, I had been, though it was four years before that, for 16 years in the public service of Canada, part of that time in a not altogether obscure position. Of necessity I knew quite intimately most of the senior public servants in this country. After I have made my proposition I would even venture to go so far as to put a direct question to the hon. member for Greenwood, who for a while was a distinguished member of the government. My impression was that in 1957 and 1958, without any exception that I know anything about, public servants-like the people of Canada, I rather suspect to tell the honest truth-had got a little bored with the government that was in office, and rather welcomed the idea of working with new people with fresh ideas. Perhaps I am wrong about that, but I gathered that impression. But I had another impression that was very much stronger, and that was that they were ready and indeed eager to do their duty and to serve their new political chiefs in the same conscientious and forthright manner in which they had served the chiefs they had before June 21, 1957.
I must say that I know of no case in which that was not true. There may have been some ardent partisans among them, but I do not know them. I certainly have never heard of any one of the distinguished public servants of this country who ever attempted in any way to thwart or even to do anything but further the policies of the government of the day. If the government of the day in some

circumstances did not have any policies to be furthered, the civil servants could hardly be blamed for that situation. However, as I say, my experience, impression or feeling was that what I have said was true; and that is what the situation should be.
In that context, if I may do so, I should like to quote from a document-I am not sure whether it is immoral or immortal- which has been quoted in this House of Commons already by the right hon. gentleman as an authority for certain conclusions which he drew from it with his usual precision, clarity and that nice capacity for making legal distinctions which sets him apart from his fellow members of the bar. I refer to the Prime Minister's use of this document in another debate, when the Prime Minister used words of mine relating to civil servants about someone who was not a civil servant at all but an officer of parliament and who, according to the Minister of Finance, was responsible to this parliament and not to any political chief, as he had no political chief. That is, of course, the kind of exact, precise, scientific, legal definition the Prime Minister gives to things. That is the way in which the Prime Minister adds so much to our understanding of the correct relationships in our constitution in these days.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I hope the hon. gentleman gets back to the bill.
I can understand that the parliamentary secretary would much rather I got back to the bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No. I shall be glad to debate that subject at any appropriate time with the hon. gentleman.
This reference was just parenthetical, Mr. Chairman. The point was that my speech which the Prime Minister did me the honour to quote and to describe as immortal-and I think he exaggerated there-
You are too modest.

As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I am afraid that I had completely forgotten about the speech until the Prime Minister dredged it up. However, I thank him. It is not the first time I have had occasion to thank the Prime Minister for advertising my literary efforts. I thank him again for advertising this one. However, I was talking about civil servants in this speech. I was not talking about officers of parliament who are suppose to be watchdogs to see that we do not have an arbitrary government. I did not expect words applied to civil servants to be taken up, torn out of their context and applied to some thing else entirely.
However, as I say, that is not the kind of argument I make or am seeking to make.
Civil Service Act
What I am seeking to do is to reinforce what I said, namely, that civil servants have certain well defined functions and duties, and that I believe the civil servants of this country, with very few exceptions and none that I know of, have performed their functions in that way.
I should like to quote one or two paragraphs from what I said about this subject. I would not have been so immodest as to do this if the Prime Minister had not cited it as an authority. I would not have thought it was an authority. It was just a fugitive speech that I made when I was invited, as a junior cabinet minister a few months after coming into office, to take part in the opening of the school of public administration at Carleton College. At that time my friend Mr. Coyne was the chairman of the board of governors of that institution. It was for that reason that my friend Mr. Coyne moved the vote of thanks. I am sure that my friend Mr. Coyne would agree completely with everything I said on that occasion, just as much now as he no doubt did then. But this was at an academic institution. Because he thanked me for making the speech he was not expected to endorse my views.
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. Could we hear something about this bill instead of the history of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate?
While the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is tending to circle somewhat, I think he is sticking reasonably closely to questions relating to the civil service.

I was just trying in passing to clear up a few misrepresentations about this speech by a very eminent member of this house. However, I wish to come back to the speech itself. Out of a relatively long experience as a public servant in this country I formed certain impressions which, since the Prime Minister considered they were worthy of note, perhaps might be worth being considered in relation to this bill. In this speech I said-
One o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, before I embark on the quotation perhaps I might call it one o'clock.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose for luncheon I was referring to this document which the Prime Minister

Civil Service Act
described first as immoral and then as immortal. I do not think it is really deserving of either epithet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: I never called it immoral.

Perhaps it was one of those errors of transcription that happen from time to time to the best of us. I was pointing out what the Prime Minister said about this speech. Of course I make no point of this, because the Prime Minister did not have the advantage of having the notes I used. There is nothing to that. The Ottawa Citizen report, which I have since examined, seems to me very fair and accurate, and I make no point of that.
However, what I did make some point of was that the Prime Minister chose to take words that I applied to civil servants and apply them to someone who was not a civil servant. That of course, in my opinion, is not a very accurate argument. I recognize this is not relevant to the present debate, but the Prime Minister did apply what I had to say about civil servants to an officer who has been described over and over again by the Minister of Finance as an officer of parliament responsible to parliament, in the same general category as the chief electoral officer, the Auditor General and those other people who are not servants of the government.
My speech referred to those people who are servants of the government, who are servants of the government of the day, under the discipline of the government of the day and having an obligation to the government of the day. Since the Prime Minister seemed to think there was some merit in what I had said, I thought I should put on the record just two or three paragraphs of what I did say on that occasion, because I do think it is very relevant to this bill, which deals with the civil service of Canada; which deals with those officials who are servants of the government and not servants of parliament or servants of crown companies.
With respect, if I may be permitted-and if anyone takes exception I will not do it, sir-to make a parenthesis with respect to the servants of crown companies, I think the original jurisprudence in this matter was established by Mr. Arthur Meighen in a very remarkable speech he made in this house in 1920; a speech with which, I may say, the Liberal party disagreed at that time but subsequently came round to accepting as the sound doctrine in relation to the C.N.R. and which every government up until very recent times has always accepted as a sound doctrine, and which I think is a sound doctrine.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Those conversions will happen in other things as well.
Yes, they do. We have had quite a history of conversions of one kind and another in this country. I think the hon. member for Carleton is, as he is wont to do, seeking to lead me away from the bill.
Oh, oh.

I think perhaps I should not yield to his seductions or temptations or whatever word he would like to apply, but should stick really strictly to this large and growing but limited class of persons who are genuine civil servants, who are and are expected to be, and have a duty to be, the servants of the government of the day; who are not, like the Auditor General, appointed to see that public funds are not misappropriated by the government; or who are not, like the governor of the Bank of Canada, appointed to see there is not inflation in secret by the government or who are not, like the chief electoral officer, appointed to see that elections are not run in the interests of a particular party. These are the necessary checks and balances that the Prime Minister and others of his associates used to talk about some years ago when they were on this side of the house, that are essential to the proper working of a constitutional system, as opposed to a notion that seems to be current in some minds, judging from some of the speeches I have heard from behind me, and perhaps from, in front of me, that if you can get a majority you can do anything you like. That is not our system.
No; there is no pipe line philosophy in this party.

As I say, there is a constant tendency in the committee to divert me from what I am trying so hard to say. I come back to that group of people who are civil servants under the Civil Service Act. I had something to say about their responsibilities, and that in my view their responsibilities were very large. Perhaps I could just quote from this document. I said: In the first place-

Order. The hon. member has come to the end of his time. Perhaps it would be agreeable to the committee for the hon. member to quote the three paragraphs he mentioned. I do not wish to interrupt him in the middle of quoting those paragraphs.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure the suggestion you have made is acceptable to the committee. In any event, now that I have intervened the hon. gentleman may go on.
Order. I do not necessarily have to recognize the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate as the next speaker. Is it agreed that the Chair's suggestion be followed?
Agreed.

I must say, Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the indulgence and the good humour of the committee, which perhaps is a nice interlude compared with some of our proceedings in recent times. I was just going to quote two or three paragraphs from this speech. I said this about civil servants:
In the first place they owe loyal and zealous service to their political chief-

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Why not put it all on the record so we will have the complete benefit of all the views of the hon. gentleman.

I am afraid I cannot really regard the Prime Minister's suggestion that my mind was limited to this document as flattering, nor do I really think the right hon. gentleman thinks quite so badly of me. Perhaps I will follow the right hon. gentleman's example and quote only selected passages.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: I meant the entire quotation, as I remember it.

I said:
In the first place they owe loyal and zealous service to their political chief so long as he enjoys the confidence of parliament. If they cannot give such service, even when they disagree with the policy, they are not entitled to feel they are doing their whole duty.
I know this can sometimes be hard, but it is sometimes hard, too, for individual ministers with strong wills and convictions to give loyal support to all the policies of the government they belong to-and yet that, too, is their duty under our system.
It is this next paragraph to which I attach great importance as a statement of the theory on which our system of government in this field, so far as the civil service is concerned, is based:
I do not think this means-or should mean-that a public servant should not honestly tell his political chief that he believes such and such a policy will have such and such bad or unfortunate effects, nor that he should not give him the full benefit of his ideas, his advice and his suggestions about policy if and when they are desired.
I believe a public servant should do his utmost to keep his political chief out of difficulties. But a public servant also has to learn that he does not make the final decisions and that the good public administrator takes his full responsibility but also knows precisely where it stops.
It was in that context and in relation to that paragraph that I also made the other semi-facetious observation which the Prime Minister quoted.

Would you read on?

semi-facetious observation which the Prime Minister quoted and which, I understand, when I was down at the railway station seeing my family off to Newfoundland yesterday, was the subject of some discussion here in the house.
One way to put it is that civil servants, like children, should be seen and not heard.
I was a civil servant for 16 years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then that, certainly, did not apply to the hon. gentleman.

This may throw some light on my character. It may be there are uncharitable members of this house on both sides who would be inclined to say that after 16 years of repression I seem to have been seeking to get over that repression. The fact of the matter is that for 16 years, after spending eight years expressing my views to audiences which paid to listen to me at the University of Manitoba, I was in the public service, and I think in the course of those 16 years I never made any public utterance of any kind which was reported in the press. To the best of my recollection I did not. I believe that on one occasion 1 read a paper to a club called the history club of the United College of the University of Manitoba. I think there were some people there besides the members of the club. But I do not think the address was reported in any newspaper and to the best of my recollection during those 16 years, while I may have expressed myself with a certain warmth at times in private- if I did not admit that I am afraid the hon. member for Essex East might rise to correct me, because he knew me in those days-my views were never expressed in public, although once or twice there was a little provocation.
These are really the only paragraphs I wanted to read. I wished to read them because it seems to me that therein lies the essence of the proper relationship between a civil servant-that is to say one who is a servant of the government, not one who is a servant of parliament-and the government. However, I think there is a corollary, and if the committee is inclined to be tolerant of me for three more sentences I should like to state that corollary. It is this. If civil servants should keep their views to themselves-and they should; if they should not make pronouncements about public policy- and in my opinion they should not-it follows equally that civil servants should not be blamed, as the Globe in its editorial of today sought to do, for the deficiencies of their political chiefs. If the political chief is to be the sole spokesman, he alone is responsible, and he is responsible for the deficiencies of

Civil Service Act
the civil servants as well as for his own deficiencies. That is the essence of our system of government.
I am not suggesting for one minute that this view has not been accepted by everyone on the treasury benches, but I do hear from time to time from certain hon. members who have not had long experience in this house the view that the government cannot be blamed for this or that because of all these wicked civil servants who will not let the government do what it wants to do. That is only a condemnation of a government; it is not a condemnation of the civil service. This, to me, is the essential point, and it is the point I have been seeking, perhaps with a few diversions, here and there, to make.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: We have been treated to a most entertaining discourse from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate pertaining to what I think I can describe as his philosophy, his approach, his attitude in regard to the relationship between public servants-
Civil servants.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: I said "public servants". The hon. member says "civil servants".
There is a difference.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
-and the government. I know the committee wishes to be entirely fair to the hon. member, and I think the only way we could be entirely fair to him would be to put on record as far as possible the entire thinking of the hon. member on the subject of this important relationship. The hon. member, with a modesty which I can only describe as being truly Pickersgillian, if I may be permitted to coin a phrase, chose to read only certain specific passages from the immortal address-I think he will agree that if it was not immortal before, it is immortal now-which he gave to the students at Carleton College on October 23, 1953, and which was reported in the Citizen the following day. There is a good deal in his address of which all of us can approve, and that is why it should be put on the record-I am serious in saying this-if I am permitted to do so. The headline reads "Pickersgill Opens New Carle-ton College Building". The report is as follows:
Marking a significant milestone in the history of Carleton College, Secretary of State J. W. Pickersgill yesterday officially opened a new school of public administration.
Now begins the report of the address:
State Secretary Pickersgill said it was impossible to be a good public servant without understanding and respecting the fundamental facts of Canadian nationhood-*
The point I wish to stress at this particular moment is that the hon. member is referring

to public servants at large, not to civil servants in a restricted sense.

I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to be unfair. I imagine I knew what I was talking about, or what I intended to say, and in any event I think the context shows what I meant, because every time I referred to public servants I also referred to their political chiefs. That speech comprehended only those public servants who have political chiefs, that is to say, those who are in a department having a political head. I want to make it very clear that that is the kind of public servant-a civil servant, in other words-to which I was referring in the whole of that speech.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my very purpose in being on my feet is to be fair to the hon. member. I wish to be fair to him in every way. The hon. member has given the committee a certain interpretation of what was said, of what is here in black and white. That is his interpretation. No one denies that that is his interpretation. Other hon. members are equally free to take whatever interpretation they might like to take from the written words. Scripta manent. The report continues:
-the fact that recognition of two official languages and two systems of jurisprudence is embedded in our constitution and the fact the nation began by tolerating two distinct but closely related cultures.
That is good. Then this article continues:
"If we are to have a good and well balanced public service in Canada, recruits must be drawn from both those original elements of our population and also from those newer elements which have been added to it", said Mr. Pickersgill.

As a matter of fact I will clear up that point right now. It was not that particular chairman, and, to tell the truth, I have completely forgotten which one it was.

That is the portion I read.

"If they cannot give such service, even when they disagree with the policy, they are not entitled to feel they are doing their whole duty," he said.
That did not mean, in his opinion, that a public servant should not honestly tell his political chief that a policy would have bad or unfortunate effects. "After all you want all the man's brains, not half of them," commented Mr. Pickersgill.

Mr. Pickersgill defined public administration as "the art of reducing a vast chaos of human relationships into some kind of order but it does not consist in my view of reducing human society to mechanical uniformity."
The state secretary said, "In public administration mere technical efficiency is no substitute for an understanding heart, but an understanding heart must be supplemented by a well furnished and inquiring mind."

Mr. Chairman, I will not need to seek unanimous consent to make a long speech, because I only have a few brief remarks to make.
